title: Insecure Deserialization and Security Misconfiguration
oneLiner: Why letting incoming data pick its own type can run an attacker's choice of code, and a pre-go-live review where you hunt for the settings that leave an app exposed.
keyTakeaway: Never let untrusted data decide which types get created: deserialize into fixed, expected types (JSON into a plain class), and never use pickle or BinaryFormatter on outside input. Most breaches need no clever exploit at all, just a default password, an open bucket or debug mode left on, so harden configuration deliberately and check it automatically.
explanation:
Serialization turns objects into text or bytes to store or send them; deserialization turns them back into objects. That second step creates objects and runs their code: constructors, property setters, and special hooks such as Python's __reduce__. If the incoming data is allowed to say which class to create, as with Newtonsoft.Json's TypeNameHandling set to All or Auto, Java's native serialization, .NET's BinaryFormatter or Python's pickle, an attacker who controls that data chooses which code runs. Real exploits chain together classes that already exist in common libraries, called gadget chains, so "we have no dangerous classes" is no defence.

The safe pattern is simple: data formats that carry only data (JSON, XML without type information), deserialized into one fixed type the code chooses, then validated. If you must hand data to a client and get it back unchanged, sign it so tampering is detected. BinaryFormatter was considered so dangerous that .NET 9 removed its implementation altogether.

Security misconfiguration is the other half of this lesson, and number two in the 2025 OWASP Top 10. It covers insecure settings rather than insecure code: debug or development mode in production (detailed error pages with stack traces), default accounts and passwords, directory listings, cloud storage left public, database ports open to the internet, permissive CORS (cross-origin resource sharing, the rules for which other websites may call your API from a browser), and sample apps nobody removed. The defence is boring and effective: build environments from version-controlled configuration (infrastructure as code), install only what you need, and scan configurations automatically.
